constants.name: K
constants.meaning: A page starts as one neutral vote (0.5) with this weight. Truth = (positive + k x 0.5) / (positive + negative + k). With k = 1 an unargued page reads 0.5, a page with one unrebutted reason moves part of the way, not all the way, to certainty.

constants.name: UNARG
constants.meaning: What a row reads for Truth when it has no page yet: a coin flip. Give it a page and the page decides.

constants.name: DEFLINK
constants.meaning: A reason placed under a conclusion is presumed relevant until a linkage page says otherwise; the burden is on the challenger. Open the linkage page ("If it were true that X, it would necessarily strengthen Y") and argue it down. The scorecard counts how many rows still rest on this presumption.

constants.name: DEFIMP
constants.meaning: The neutral start for importance, the wiki's own rule: an importance nobody has argued opens at 0.5, neither trivial nor decisive, until an importance page names the issues the row addresses and their argued importance takes over. Not a penalty; the absence of a claim either way.

constants.name: DEFUNIQ
constants.meaning: A reason is presumed distinct until a uniqueness page shows the overlap.

pages.text: Ending single-family-only zoning lowers housing costs in the cities that do it.
pages.bottom_line: The agree side leads on evidence from Auckland, Minneapolis and the spillover studies; the honest con is that upzoning without cheaper construction produces little where land is dearest.
pages.logical_form: (Zoning is the binding constraint on supply in high-cost cities) AND (more supply lowers prices). The normative component (lower prices are the right goal) is separable.

pages.text: Where cities have allowed more homes per lot, permits rose and rents grew more slowly than in comparable cities that did not.
pages.bottom_line: Three cities point the same way; the open question is how much of each divergence the single-family change itself explains.

pages.text: Housing prices track the gap between demand and the number of homes; zoning that caps homes per lot is the binding constraint on supply in high-cost metros.
pages.bottom_line: The premium evidence is strong for coastal metros; construction cost is a serious rival explanation in the 2020s.

pages.text: New market-rate homes lower rents in nearby existing buildings by pulling higher-income renters out of older housing.
pages.bottom_line: The replicated finding is a small local rent decrease; the contested part is what happens to the very cheapest nearby buildings.

pages.text: Allowing duplexes and small apartments on single-family lots adds homes without public subsidy, so it is the cheapest affordability tool available.
pages.bottom_line: True on public cost per unit; the disagree side is right that it is a slow tool for the poorest renters.

pages.text: Upzoning alone produces few homes where land is expensive and construction costs are high; California's 2021 lot-split law produced only a few hundred units in its first two years.
pages.bottom_line: Right about SB 9 and about the cost environment; weaker as a general claim, since better-designed reforms are producing rising counts.

pages.text: Allowing more units raises land values, which can raise the price of existing homes and displace lower-income owners and renters through redevelopment.
pages.bottom_line: The land-value effect is real; the displacement claim runs against the better evidence.

pages.text: Neighborhood character, parking, school crowding and infrastructure capacity are real costs that fall on existing residents while the benefits go to newcomers.
pages.bottom_line: Some costs are real and mostly unpriced; whether they bear on housing costs is decided on the linkage page (tab 14).

pages.text: Rents in Minneapolis and Austin also fell because of a building boom financed by cheap money in 2021-2022, which is not repeatable.
pages.bottom_line: Right about Austin's timing, weak on Minneapolis; the two causes are not exclusive.

pages.text: Minneapolis rents grew far more slowly than the rest of Minnesota from 2017 to 2023 because of its 2019 zoning and parking reforms.
pages.bottom_line: The divergence is real; how much of it the single-family change explains is open, and the 2017 start is the strongest objection.

pages.bridge: Renters in existing buildings, whose rents the new homes pull down.
X adds a comparison of public cost per home against subsidy programs; Z says nothing about what the reform costs the public.
pages.bottom_line: The cost comparison is new, the mechanism is shared.

pages.text: Upzoning along Chicago transit corridors in 2013 and 2015 raised land values and prices without increasing construction, which shows upzoning can raise housing costs.
pages.bottom_line: A solid finding about small corridor upzonings; it says little about citywide reform.

pages.bridge: Costs to existing residents would weaken the belief only if they raised housing costs or got the reform repealed; on their own they are a separate cost.
pages.bottom_line: Low linkage: a true argument aimed at a different question. It counts fully in the cost-benefit table.

pages.bridge: Existing residents, who bear the parking, school and infrastructure costs.

pages.text: Some homeowners want to keep lower-income households out of their neighborhood.
pages.measured_by: Income mix of new residents in reformed neighborhoods against the existing residents
pages.if_true: Lower-income households move in as costs fall
pages.latest: Not yet measured for reformed single-family neighborhoods
pages.bottom_line: Held by some, valid by almost no standard; kept on the page so the scoring is visible.

pages.bridge: The work measures the price of permission; the belief is about removing one kind of permission.
pages.bottom_line: Bearing: does the work speak to this belief at all?

pages.text: Ending single-family-only zoning leaves rents in reform cities about 5 percent below the counterfactual after five years.
pages.bottom_line: Plausible where building follows; the magnitude is an estimate, not a measurement.

pages.text: Ending single-family-only zoning adds about 3 homes per 1,000 residents per year without public subsidy.
pages.bottom_line: Auckland-scale reforms reach the number; timid ones do not.

pages.text: Infill housing from zoning reform cuts vehicle miles per new resident by about 20 percent compared with the same growth at the urban edge.
pages.bottom_line: Well supported for the residents who would otherwise live at the edge; the counterfactual is the soft spot.

pages.text: Ending single-family-only zoning reduces the value of existing single-family homes by about 3 percent where new homes compete with them.
pages.bottom_line: Runs against the evidence: upzoning has raised, not lowered, existing values in the cases studied.

pages.text: Redevelopment under zoning reform displaces about 50 households per 1,000 new units built.
pages.bottom_line: Direct demolition displacement is real but small for middle housing; the net effect may be negative.

pages.text: Each new unit from zoning reform imposes about 20,000 dollars of school, parking and utility costs on built-out neighborhoods.
pages.bottom_line: Some cost is real; the figure is high against what cost-of-service studies show.

pages.text: Renters and first-time buyers need housing prices they can afford.
pages.measured_by: Share of renters paying more than 30 percent of income on housing, reform cities against matched cities
pages.if_true: Falls in reform cities against matched cities
pages.latest: About half of renters nationally (Census ACS); not yet compared for reform cities
pages.bottom_line: Near the top of any hierarchy of needs; validity is not seriously contested.

pages.text: Current homeowners need to protect the value of their homes.
pages.measured_by: Resale price of existing single-family homes near new multiplexes, against comparable homes with no new neighbors
pages.if_true: Slightly lower where new homes compete
pages.latest: Mixed: land value up on upzoned lots, resale effects on neighbors small so far (Freemark 2020; Sightline 2023)
pages.bottom_line: Valid as security, weaker as a claim to control what neighbors build.

pages.text: Allowing up to four units on every residential lot by right, with design standards and no parking minimums, with infrastructure funded from the added tax base, would satisfy the main interests of both sides.
pages.bottom_line: The most-adopted middle ground; parking is where it succeeds or fails.

pages.text: More housing supply lowers prices and rents relative to the counterfactual.
pages.bottom_line: The basic economics holds up; induced demand slows the effect without erasing it.

pages.text: Lower housing costs are the right goal even where current owners lose value.
pages.bottom_line: A values ranking, not a fact; the page scores the arguments for each ranking.

pages.text: Builders respond to permission with construction at prices below current rents.
pages.bottom_line: True in most reform cities; false so far in California's narrow reform.

pages.text: New supply mainly serves higher-income newcomers rather than filtering down.
pages.bottom_line: True about first occupants, false about where the vacancy chain ends.

pages.text: Supporters' advertised reason (more homes, lower rents) differs from their actual driver (developer returns).
pages.bottom_line: Partly true for some funders, not for the movement.

pages.text: Opponents' advertised reason (neighborhood character) differs from their actual driver (home equity and exclusion).
pages.bottom_line: Well supported as a tendency; not true of every opponent.

pages.text: The benefits of zoning reform arrive years after the political fight, which makes the reform hard to sustain.
pages.bottom_line: A real obstacle: the costs are immediate and the benefits are slow.

pages.text: Opponents cannot point to a high-cost city that fixed affordability without adding supply, which weakens their position.
pages.bottom_line: Holds, with Vienna as the exception that added supply by other means.

pages.text: Abolishing zoning entirely would lower housing costs.
pages.bottom_line: The more extreme cousin of the belief; it inherits the supply evidence and adds costs the parent does not.

pages.text: Ending single-family-only zoning slows rent growth modestly in high-demand cities and changes little elsewhere.
pages.bottom_line: The version of the belief most of the evidence supports directly.

pages.text: After Auckland upzoned about three quarters of its residential land in 2016, dwelling consents in upzoned areas rose sharply relative to trend, adding an estimated 20,000-plus homes in five years.
pages.bottom_line: A peer-reviewed finding with a clear design; the completions caveat is the main open point.

pages.text: Austin permitted more apartments per resident than any large U.S. metro in 2021-2023, and asking rents fell more than 15 percent from their 2023 peak by 2025.
pages.bottom_line: The permit ranking and the rent decline are both well documented; the size of the sitting-tenant effect is not.

pages.text: New apartment buildings in New York, San Francisco and Helsinki lowered rents in buildings within a few hundred meters by 1 to 6 percent relative to controls.
pages.bottom_line: Replicated across cities; the lowest-rent tier is the contested corner.

pages.text: A UC Berkeley Terner Center review found fewer than 500 SB 9 applications statewide in the law's first year, concentrated in a handful of cities.
pages.bottom_line: Well documented; the number is low by any count.

pages.bridge: The work describes the belief's outcome in the best-known reform city.
pages.bottom_line: Bearing: does the work speak to this belief at all?

pages.bridge: The work is the belief's outcome reversed, in a setting that may not compare.
pages.bottom_line: Bearing: does the work speak to this belief at all?

pages.text: Land values rise on upzoned lots before construction starts.
pages.bottom_line: Well established.

pages.text: Permit applications rise within a year of reform where the rules are simple.
pages.bottom_line: True conditional on simple rules.

pages.text: Rents settle below the counterfactual as supply accumulates over a decade.
pages.bottom_line: The central long-run prediction; the data will arrive around 2030.

pages.text: Neighborhoods gain small apartment buildings and lose some detached homes over a decade.
pages.bottom_line: Directionally certain, small in magnitude.

pages.text: Builders need permission to build what the market will buy.
pages.measured_by: Homes permitted per 1,000 residents per year in reform cities against matched cities
pages.latest: Auckland: consents roughly doubled in upzoned areas, 2016-2021 (Greenaway-McGrevy and Phillips 2023)
pages.bottom_line: Valid as an economic interest; weaker as a claim on policy priority.

pages.text: Residents of older neighborhoods need protection from displacement by redevelopment.
pages.measured_by: Households moving out within 500 meters of redevelopment, per 1,000 new units, against control blocks
pages.if_true: No higher than controls as rents ease
pages.latest: Lower near new construction in San Francisco (Pennington 2021); not measured for middle housing
pages.bottom_line: A valid need whose size is contested.

pages.text: Both sides want their children able to afford to live in the city they grew up in.
pages.bottom_line: About as shared as interests get.

pages.text: Supply optimism (assuming permission alone produces homes) biases supporters of zoning reform.
pages.bottom_line: Real, and easy to see in California.

pages.text: Status-quo bias and loss aversion about home values bias opponents of zoning reform.
pages.bottom_line: Well supported as a tendency.

pages.text: Cities that reformed in 2019-2023 will show slower rent growth than matched cities through 2030.
pages.bottom_line: The central pending test of the belief.

pages.text: Reform and non-reform cities will show the same rent trajectories once interest rates and migration are controlled for.
pages.bottom_line: The rival's prediction; the controlled comparison will decide it.

pages.text: Minneapolis rents will grow more slowly than the Minnesota average in the five years after the 2019 reform.
pages.bottom_line: Confirmed as stated; attribution remains partly open.

pages.text: California's SB 9 lot splits will add thousands of homes within two years of taking effect.
pages.bottom_line: Disconfirmed; the failed prediction counts against the belief.

pages.text: Glaeser and Gyourko, The Economic Implications of Housing Supply (2018)
pages.bridge: Zoning and other rules keep prices far above construction cost in coastal metros.
pages.bottom_line: Foundational for the supply argument.

pages.text: Pew Charitable Trusts, Minneapolis housing analysis (2024)
pages.bridge: Minneapolis rents lagged the state after 2019 while its housing stock grew faster.
pages.bottom_line: The best-known case, descriptively strong, causally open.

pages.text: Freemark, Upzoning Chicago (2020)
pages.bridge: Small corridor upzonings raised land prices without adding construction within five years.
pages.bottom_line: A real caution about small upzonings.

pages.text: Minneapolis 2040 (2019), Oregon HB 2001 (2019) and California SB 9 (2021) and SB 79 (2025) assume that ending single-family-only zoning lowers housing costs.
pages.bottom_line: Institutional agreement, documented; not proof.

pages.text: Local zoning authority under state enabling acts and environmental review statutes complicate the belief that ending single-family-only zoning lowers housing costs.
pages.bottom_line: The legal machinery cuts both ways and is moving.

pages.text: Prices fall when supply is allowed to meet demand.
pages.bottom_line: The upstream principle the belief inherits from.

pages.text: Local communities should control what gets built near them.
pages.bottom_line: A values claim; the outcomes evidence leans against it.

pages.text: Parking minimums should be abolished near transit.
pages.bottom_line: A downstream belief that inherits most of this page's logic.

pages.text: Historic districts should be exempt from upzoning.
pages.bottom_line: Defensible for buildings, abused for neighborhoods.

pages.text: Edward Glaeser is on record that regulation, including zoning, raises housing prices.
pages.bottom_line: Documented.

pages.text: The Pew Charitable Trusts housing policy initiative is on record that zoning reform lowers housing costs.
pages.bottom_line: Documented.

pages.text: Livable California is on record opposing SB 9 and SB 50.
pages.bottom_line: Documented.

pages.text: Yonah Freemark is on record that upzoning can raise prices without adding housing.
pages.bottom_line: On record for the narrow finding, not against reform in general.

pages.text: A multi-city study shows rents falling relative to matched controls after zoning reform, with the effect growing over time.
pages.bottom_line: Pending: the study that would settle the belief has not been done.

pages.text: Reform cities' price-to-construction-cost premium shrinks in the years after reform.
pages.bottom_line: Pending, and ambiguous unless construction costs are held constant.

pages.text: Reform cities' rents tracked non-reform cities once the 2021-2022 construction boom is controlled for.
pages.bottom_line: Pending; the Austin and Minneapolis cases pull in opposite directions.

pages.text: Upzoned single-family lots were redeveloped mainly into larger single homes rather than into more units.
pages.bottom_line: Pending; early permit data lean against it.

pages.text: Newcomers and young families need somewhere to live in the city.
pages.measured_by: Homes added per 1,000 residents per year and the rental vacancy rate, reform cities against matched cities
pages.if_true: Homes added rise and vacancy loosens
pages.latest: Minneapolis added housing faster than the rest of Minnesota, 2017-2023 (Pew 2024)
pages.bottom_line: As basic as needs get; contested only on who gets a say.

pages.text: Commuters and the climate need homes near jobs rather than at the urban edge.
pages.measured_by: Vehicle miles per new resident, infill homes against homes at the urban edge
pages.latest: Infill households drive less than edge households in every study cited on the benefit page; the margin varies
pages.bottom_line: Real and diffuse; it rarely drives anyone to a hearing.

pages.text: Existing residents need to keep the neighborhood character, parking and school capacity they have.
pages.measured_by: Street parking occupancy and school enrollment against capacity in reformed neighborhoods
pages.if_true: Within capacity, funded by the added tax base
pages.if_false: Over capacity, with infrastructure bills following
pages.bottom_line: Real costs, mostly unpriced; weaker as a claim on others' lots.

edges.text: In the most regulated metros the price of a home exceeds its construction cost by a large regulatory premium, while in lightly regulated metros price tracks construction cost.
Metros that allow building (Houston, Atlanta, Dallas) absorbed large demand booms with prices near construction cost, which a demand-only story cannot explain.
Where lots allow only one home, the land price per home is the whole lot, so the cap on units is what makes the land unaffordable.
Construction costs and financing, not zoning, are the binding constraint in many cities: hard costs rose faster than rents in 2015-2023.
In cities with weak demand, upzoning changes nothing because nobody wants to build; zoning binds only where demand already outruns supply.

Glaeser and Gyourko estimate that in the most regulated metros home prices exceed minimum profitable production cost by a large margin, while in lightly regulated metros the two are close.
Glaeser and Gyourko, Journal of Economic Perspectives (2018)

Metros with elastic housing supply saw smaller price booms and smaller busts in the 2000s cycle.
Glaeser, Gyourko and Saiz, Journal of Urban Economics (2008)

Multifamily hard construction costs in California rose by roughly a third to a half between 2015 and 2023, outpacing rents in most markets.
Terner Center for Housing Innovation, construction cost reports (2020-2024)
